```{r}
#| label: setup

library(SigBridgeR)
library(Seurat)
```

# Overview

Accuracy and biological signal are only part of the story: a method that takes
hours and tens of gigabytes is often impractical, even when it performs well.
`BenchMemory()` runs every configured screening method on the same inputs and
records wall time and memory for each run.

A benchmark is organised in **rounds**. Within one round every method is
screened once. By default the order of methods is shuffled in each round, so
cold caches, lazy package loading and package-level caches are spread across
methods instead of always penalising whichever method happens to run first.

Each measurement runs in its own background R process created with
`callr::r_bg()`. The inputs are serialised once into a temporary directory and
loaded by each child, so one method cannot leak loaded Python runtimes, package
caches or large result objects into the next measurement.

# Building a configuration

`BenchMemory()` takes a `BenchMemoryConfig`, which combines the shared
benchmark inputs with the controls returned by `BenchMemoryConfigSet()`:

```{r}
#| label: benchmemory-config-small
tiny_sc <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = Matrix::Matrix(
    matrix(
      seq_len(20L),
      nrow = 5L,
      dimnames = list(paste0("Gene", 1:5), paste0("Cell", 1:4))
    ),
    sparse = TRUE
  )
)

config <- BenchMemoryConfig(
  matched_bulk = matrix(
    seq_len(5L),
    nrow = 5L,
    dimnames = list(paste0("Gene", 1:5), "Sample1")
  ),
  sc_data = tiny_sc,
  phenotype = c(Sample1 = 1),
  label_type = "{method_name}",
  phenotype_class = "binary",
  screen_method = "scPP",
  method_param = MethodParamSet(
    scPP_param = list(Log2FC_cutoff = 0.585)
  ),
  bench_config = BenchMemoryConfigSet(
    rounds = 3L,
    order = "random",
    probe_resources = FALSE
  )
)

config@screen_method
config@bench_config[c("rounds", "order", "probe_resources")]
```

The same structure is used for a real benchmark. The only difference is the
size of the inputs and the number of methods:

```{r}
#| label: benchmemory-config
#| eval: false
config <- BenchMemoryConfig(
  matched_bulk = bulk,
  sc_data = sc,
  phenotype = phenotype,
  label_type = "{method_name}",
  phenotype_class = "binary",
  screen_method = c("scPP", "scPAS", "LP_SGL"),
  method_param = MethodParamSet(
    scPP_param = list(Log2FC_cutoff = 0.585),
    scPAS_param = list(permutation_times = 500)
  ),
  bench_config = BenchMemoryConfigSet(
    rounds = 3L,
    order = "random",
    measure_rss = TRUE,
    set_threads = 1L,
    timeout_sec = 1800
  )
)
```

`method_param` has one field per registered method and each field is passed only
to the method it is named after. Use `MethodParamSet()` to get the full set of
empty defaults and fill in only the methods you need.

# Running the benchmark

```{r}
#| label: benchmemory-run
#| eval: false
res <- BenchMemory(config, verbose = FALSE)
```

The result is a `data.table` with one row per method per round. It contains the
columns returned by `bench::mark()` (`min`, `median`, `itr/sec`, `mem_alloc`,
`n_itr`, `n_gc`, `total_time`, ...), plus the benchmark bookkeeping columns:

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `method_name` | Screening method |
| `round` | Round number |
| `position` | Position of the method within the round |
| `status` | `"ok"`, `"error"` or `"timeout"` |
| `error` | Error message for failed measurements |
| `mem_peak_mb` | Peak R heap high-water mark in MB |
| `rss_peak_mb` | Peak process resident set size in MB (`measure_rss = TRUE`, Linux only) |
| `elapsed` | Wall-clock seconds spent by the measurement |

Successful measurements have `status = "ok"`. Failed or timed-out measurements
are kept with `status = "error"` or `"timeout"`, an `error` message and `NA`
memory metrics, so one broken method does not silently disappear.

# Summarising the result

Timing is naturally variable, so summarise across rounds rather than reading a
single row. `median` is a `difftime`; convert it to seconds before aggregating:

```{r}
#| label: benchmemory-summary
#| eval: false
ok <- res[res$status == "ok", ]
ok$median_sec <- as.numeric(ok$median)

aggregate(
  cbind(median_sec, mem_peak_mb, rss_peak_mb) ~ method_name,
  data = ok,
  FUN = median
)
```

The same summary with `data.table`:

```{r}
#| label: benchmemory-summary-dt
#| eval: false
res[
  status == "ok",
  .(
    median_sec = median(as.numeric(median)),
    mem_peak_mb = median(mem_peak_mb),
    rss_peak_mb = median(rss_peak_mb),
    rounds = .N
  ),
  by = method_name
]
```

If a method failed, inspect those rows before drawing conclusions:

```{r}
#| label: benchmemory-failures
#| eval: false
res[status != "ok", c("method_name", "round", "status", "error"), with = FALSE]
```

# Benchmark controls

`BenchMemoryConfigSet()` collects and validates the controls. The most
important ones are:

| Control | Default | Purpose |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `rounds` | `3L` | Number of times every method is screened |
| `order` | `"random"` | Shuffle methods within each round, or keep `"fixed"` order |
| `seed` | package seed | Base seed for shuffling and for each measurement child |
| `timeout_sec` | `10800L` | Maximum seconds for one method in one round |
| `on_failure` | `"skip"` | Record the failure and continue, or `"stop"` the whole benchmark |
| `set_threads` | `1L` | Pin each child process to this many threads |
| `measure_rss` | `FALSE` | Also record peak process RSS (Linux only) |
| `probe_resources` | `TRUE` | Collect a machine resource summary before staging the inputs |
| `min_iterations`, `max_iterations` | `1L`, `1L` | Iteration bounds for `bench::mark()` |
| `memory`, `filter_gc`, `check`, `min_time`, `relative`, `time_unit` | `bench::mark()` defaults | Forwarded to `bench::mark()` |

A few practical choices:

* **Use at least three rounds.** A single round mixes genuine cost with
  one-off startup effects. Odd round counts also let the median ignore one
  unusually slow round.
* **Keep `order = "random"`.** It prevents the first method in the list from
  systematically paying for cold caches. The shuffle is reproducible because
  `seed` plus the round number is used.
* **Pin threads when comparing methods.** `set_threads = 1L` avoids a method
  that internally uses many threads from looking faster merely because it
  consumed more cores. Record the setting alongside the results.
* **Set a realistic timeout.** A hung Python backend or an accidental
  full-data copy should not block the benchmark for days.
* **`probe_resources = FALSE`** skips the initial `gc()` and machine probe,
  which is useful when the workspace is very large and startup time matters.

# Interpreting the numbers

Three memory numbers are reported because they describe different things:

* `mem_alloc` is the total allocated during the run, i.e. allocation churn. A
  method can allocate a lot and still keep a small peak.
* `mem_peak_mb` is the peak R heap high-water mark. It is reset before each
  measurement and is usually the best indicator of R-side peak memory.
* `rss_peak_mb` is the peak resident set size of the whole process. It also
  includes native libraries, Python runtimes and memory mapped files, so it is
  closer to what a scheduler will reserve.

Compare methods measured on the same machine, with the same data, thread count
and package versions. Absolute timings are not portable across machines, but
the relative ranking is often stable.

# See also

* `BenchMemoryConfig()` and `BenchMemoryConfigSet()` for the configuration
  interface.
* `BenchAcc()`, `BenchGSEA()` and `BenchGeneScore()` for accuracy, functional
  signal and cell-level pathway scores.
* `bench::mark()` for the timing and allocation measurements.
